claim: 48 short antisense DNA oligonucleotide probes were designed to target the viral ORF1a and labelled with a single fluorescent dye to detect the positive sense gRNA.
source: 48 short antisense DNA oligonucleotide probes were designed to target the viral ORF1a and labelled with a single fluorescent dye to detect the positive sense gRNA, as described previously (Gaspar et al., 2017; Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design and cites a previous publication (Gaspar et al., 2017) for the methodology.

claim: The probe set detected single molecules of gRNA within SARS-CoV-2-infected Vero E6 cells, visible as well-resolved diffraction-limited single spots with a consistent fluorescence intensity and shape.
source: The probe set detected single molecules of gRNA within SARS-CoV-2-infected Vero E6 cells, visible as well-resolved diffraction-limited single spots with a consistent fluorescence intensity and shape (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and reference to Figure 1B showing the imaging data.

claim: Treatment of the infected cells with RNase or the viral polymerase inhibitor remdesivir (RDV) ablated the probe signal, confirming specificity.
source: Treatment of the infected cells with RNase or the viral polymerase inhibitor remdesivir (RDV) ablated the probe signal, confirming specificity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of signal upon RNase or RDV treatment, referenced in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 95% of the diffraction-limited spots within infected cells were dual labelled, demonstrating efficient detection of single SARS-CoV-2 gRNA molecules.
source: 95% of the diffraction-limited spots within infected cells were dual labelled, demonstrating efficient detection of single SARS-CoV-2 gRNA molecules (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dual-labeling experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The +ORF1a probes detected SARS-CoV-2 gRNA in a representative section of the infected lung tissue, showing variable intracellular RNA levels within the lung tissue.
source: The +ORF1a probes detected SARS-CoV-2 gRNA in a representative section of the infected lung tissue, showing variable intracellular RNA levels within the lung tissue (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by smFISH data from FFPE hamster lung tissue shown in Figure 1E.

claim: At 2 hr post infection (hpi), most fluorescent spots correspond to single gRNAs along with a small number of foci harbouring several gRNA copies.
source: At 2 hr post infection (hpi), most fluorescent spots correspond to single gRNAs along with a small number of foci harbouring several gRNA copies (Figure 1F), consistent with early RNA replication events.
evidence: The claim is supported by smFISH imaging data at 2 hpi shown in Figure 1F.

claim: By 8 hpi, there was an expansion in the number of bright multi-gRNA foci.
source: By 8 hpi, we noted an expansion in the number of bright multi-gRNA foci, and at 24 hpi there was a further increase in the number of multi-RNA foci that localised to the perinuclear region (Figure 1F); consistent with the reported association of viral replication factories with membranous structures derived from the endoplasmic reticulum (V'kovski et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course imaging data in Figure 1F and is consistent with published literature (V'kovski et al., 2021).

claim: At 24 hpi there was a further increase in the number of multi-RNA foci that localised to the perinuclear region.
source: By 8 hpi, we noted an expansion in the number of bright multi-gRNA foci, and at 24 hpi there was a further increase in the number of multi-RNA foci that localised to the perinuclear region (Figure 1F); consistent with the reported association of viral replication factories with membranous structures derived from the endoplasmic reticulum (V'kovski et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data at 24 hpi shown in Figure 1F and is consistent with published literature.

claim: Individual gRNA molecules at the periphery of cells are consistent with individual viral particles observed at the same location by electron microscopy.
source: Interestingly, our observation of individual gRNA molecules at the periphery of cells (Figure 1F) is also consistent with individual viral particles observed at the same location by electron microscopy (Cortese et al., 2020; Klein et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by smFISH observations in Figure 1F and is consistent with electron microscopy studies cited (Cortese et al., 2020; Klein et al., 2020).

claim: A high abundance of sgRNAs was observed compared to gRNAs in infected Vero E6 cells at 6 hpi.
source: We applied this approach to visualise SARS-CoV-2 RNAs in infected Vero E6 cells (6 hpi) and observed a high abundance of sgRNAs compared to gRNAs (Figure 2B), in agreement with RNA sequencing studies (Alexandersen et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 2B and is consistent with RNA sequencing studies (Alexandersen et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020).

claim: The +ORFN single-labelled sgRNAs were more uniformly dispersed throughout the cytoplasm than dual-labelled gRNA.
source: Further analysis revealed that the +ORFN single-labelled sgRNAs were more uniformly dispersed throughout the cytoplasm than dual-labelled gRNA, consistent with their predominant role as mRNAs to direct protein synthesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with the known function of sgRNAs.

claim: gRNAs were enriched near the periphery of the nucleus in a clustered fashion.
source: However, gRNAs were enriched near the periphery of the nucleus in a clustered fashion.
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial distribution analysis of smFISH data.

claim: N protein primarily co-localises with gRNA, while displaying a limited overlap with sgRNAs.
source: Our findings show that N protein primarily co-localises with gRNA, while displaying a limited overlap with sgRNAs (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization analysis shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Negative sense gRNA spots were detected at a significantly lower level than their +gRNA counterparts.
source: The -gRNA spots were detected at a significantly lower level than their +gRNA counterparts, with substantial overlap observed between the two strands at multi-RNA spots, consistent with these foci representing active sites of viral replication.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of positive and negative strand detection by smFISH.

claim: Substantial overlap was observed between positive and negative strand gRNA at multi-RNA spots, consistent with these foci representing active sites of viral replication.
source: The -gRNA spots were detected at a significantly lower level than their +gRNA counterparts, with substantial overlap observed between the two strands at multi-RNA spots, consistent with these foci representing active sites of viral replication.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization analysis of positive and negative strand gRNA and is consistent with the biology of viral replication.

claim: RNaseT1 digestion diminished the +ORF1a probe signal, while RNaseIII treatment abolished the anti-dsRNA J2 signal.
source: RNaseT1 digestion diminished the +ORF1a probe signal, while RNaseIII treatment abolished the anti-dsRNA J2 signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNase digestion experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: A cocktail of RNaseT1 and RNaseIII ablated both +ORF1a probe binding and anti-dsRNA J2 signals.
source: A cocktail of RNaseT1 and RNaseIII ablated both +ORF1a probe binding and anti-dsRNA J2 signals, demonstrating that the +ORF1a probe set hybridises to both single and duplex RNA under our experimental conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNase digestion experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Treating cells with DMSO prior to RNaseT1 fully ablated the smFISH signal.
source: Furthermore, treating cells with DMSO prior to RNaseT1 fully ablated the smFISH signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), demonstrating that denaturation makes dsRNA accessible for RNaseT1 degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Probe binding to negative strand gRNA requires chemical denaturation, suggesting that this replication intermediate is rich in dsRNA structures.
source: In summary, our data show that probe binding to negative strand gRNA requires chemical denaturation, suggesting that this replication intermediate is rich in dsRNA structures.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the requirement of DMSO denaturation for negative strand detection.

claim: No viral-specific J2 signal was detected at 2 hpi, and only 10% of infected cells stained positive at 6 hpi.
source: No viral-specific J2 signal was detected at 2 hpi, and only 10% of infected cells stained positive at 6 hpi, in agreement with previous observations (Cortese et al., 2020; Eymieux et al., 2021; Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of J2 staining shown in Figure 2E and is consistent with previous studies (Cortese et al., 2020; Eymieux et al., 2021).

claim: More than 85% of the cells showed diffraction-limited smFISH signals at both 2 and 6 hpi.
source: In contrast, more than 85% of the cells showed diffraction-limited smFISH signals at both timepoints (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of smFISH-positive cells shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The average J2 signal detected in the SARS-CoV-2-infected cells at both 2 and 6 hpi was comparable to uninfected cells.
source: Furthermore, the average J2 signal detected in the SARS-CoV-2-infected cells at both timepoints was comparable to uninfected cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of J2 signal intensity shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The J2 antibody underestimates the frequency of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: These data clearly show that the J2 antibody, although broadly used, underestimates the frequency of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison between J2 antibody detection and smFISH detection rates.

claim: smFISH detected gRNA as early as 2 hpi, with a significant increase in copy number by 6 hpi.
source: In contrast, smFISH detected gRNA as early as 2 hpi, with a significant increase in copy number by 6 hpi, highlighting its utility to detect and quantify viral replication factories.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course quantification of gRNA by smFISH.

claim: At 2 hpi, the +ORF1a probe set detected predominantly single molecules of +gRNA with a median value of ~30 molecules per cell.
source: At 2 hpi, the +ORF1a probe set detected predominantly single molecules of +gRNA with a median value of ~30 molecules per cell (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: At 2 hpi RDV treatment did not affect the number of gRNA copies per cell, suggesting that these RNAs derive from incoming viral particles.
source: Interestingly, at 2 hpi RDV treatment did not affect the number of gRNA copies per cell, suggesting that these RNAs derive from incoming viral particles (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of gRNA counts in untreated and RDV-treated cells at 2 hpi shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The increase in gRNA copies per cell at 4 and 6 hpi was inhibited by RDV, indicating active viral replication.
source: In contrast, the increase in gRNA copies per cell at 4 and 6 hpi was inhibited by RDV, indicating active viral replication.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of gRNA counts in untreated and RDV-treated cells at 4 and 6 hpi.

claim: The infected cell population showed varying gRNA levels that were classified into three groups: 'partially resistant' cells with <102 gRNA copies (60% of the population), 'permissive' cells with ~102–105 copies per cell (~30%), and 'super-permissive' cells with >105 copies per cell (~10%).
source: The infected cell population showed varying gRNA levels that we classified into three groups; (i) 'partially resistant' cells with <102 gRNA copies that showed no increase in gRNA burden between 2 and 8 hpi (60% of the population); (ii) 'permissive' cells with ~102–105 copies per cell showing a modest increase over time (~30%); and (iii) 'super-permissive' cells with >105 copies per cell showing a sharp increase in gRNA copies (~10%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of gRNA distribution across the cell population.

claim: 'Super-permissive' cells are the dominant source of gRNA across the culture.
source: Analysing the total cellular gRNA content showed that 'super-permissive' cells are the dominant source of gRNA across the culture (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of total gRNA contribution by cell type shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Bulk RNA analyses such as RT-qPCR are biased towards the high gRNA burden group.
source: This suggests that bulk RNA analyses such as RT-qPCR are biased towards this high gRNA burden group.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that super-permissive cells contribute most of the total gRNA.

claim: Cellular heterogeneity persists beyond the initial hours of infection, with 40% of cells not reaching the super-permissive state even at 24 hpi.
source: Importantly, we found that cellular heterogeneity persists beyond the initial hours of infection. Even at 24 hpi, 40% of the cells did not reach the super-permissive state, and they formed a distinct population with approximately 10-fold less gRNA (Figure 3C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of gRNA distribution at 24 hpi shown in Figure 3C and E.

claim: The high level of gRNA content in super-permissive cells (~107 counts/cell) was similar throughout the time course, suggesting the existence of an upper limit of gRNA copies in Vero E6 cells.
source: Notably, the high level of gRNA content in super-permissive cells (~107 counts/cell) was similar throughout the time course, suggesting the existence of an upper limit of gRNA copies in Vero E6 cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of gRNA in super-permissive cells across the time course shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The average number of gRNA copies per cell was stable in RDV-treated cells, suggesting that the incoming gRNA is long-lived.
source: Notably, the average number of gRNA copies per cell was stable in RDV-treated cells (Figure 3C), suggesting that the incoming gRNA is long-lived.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course analysis of gRNA in RDV-treated cells shown in Figure 3C.

claim: RDV treatment led to a reduced proportion of super-permissive cells and non-viable cells at 48 hpi, indicating an inhibition of viral replication and viral-induced cell death.
source: As expected, RDV treatment led to a reduced proportion of super-permissive cells and non-viable cells at 48 hpi, indicating an inhibition of viral replication and, consequently, viral-induced cell death (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Considerable levels of gRNA persisted in RDV-treated cells even after 24 hr of treatment, suggesting that gRNA is relatively stable at late times post infection.
source: However, considerable levels of gRNA persisted in these cells even after 24 hr of RDV treatment, suggesting that gRNA is also relatively stable at late times post infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course analysis of gRNA in RDV-treated cells.

claim: The half-life of gRNA in late infection was estimated to be within a range of 6–8 hr.
source: To estimate the half-life of gRNA in late infection, we fitted a decay curve and calculated the half-life of gRNA within a range of 6–8 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by decay curve analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 11 copies/cell of sgRNA were detected in 63% of infected cells at 2 hpi.
source: Simultaneous analysis of +ORF1a and +ORFN revealed similar expression kinetics for sgRNA, with 11 copies/cell of sgRNA detected in 63% of infected cells at 2 hpi (Figure 3C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C and F.

claim: The detection of sgRNA at 2 hpi implies that multiple rounds of transcription occur rapidly following virus internalisation that are RDV insensitive.
source: Since +sgRNA requires -sgRNA template for its production, our results imply that multiple rounds of transcription occur rapidly following virus internalisation that are RDV insensitive.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the detection of sgRNA at 2 hpi and the requirement of negative strand template for sgRNA synthesis.

claim: By 6 hpi, most cells contain sgRNA.
source: By 6 hpi, most cells contain sgRNA (Figure 3F), with the super-permissive cells supporting high levels of sgRNA transcription.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The sgRNA/gRNA ratio ranged from 0.5 to 8 over time.
source: We examined the vRNA replication dynamics and found the ratio of sgRNA/gRNA ranged from 0.5 to 8 over time (Figure 3G), consistent with a recent report in diagnostic samples (Alexandersen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3G and is consistent with published data (Alexandersen et al., 2020).

claim: The sgRNA/gRNA ratio increased between 2 and 10 hpi, followed by a decline at 24 hpi, indicating a shift in preference to produce gRNA over sgRNA in later stages of infection.
source: Notably, the sgRNA/gRNA ratio increased between 2 and 10 hpi, followed by a decline at 24 hpi, indicating a shift in preference to produce gRNA over sgRNA in later stages of infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course analysis of sgRNA/gRNA ratio.

claim: sgRNA synthesis is favoured in the 'partially resistant' and 'permissive' cells, whereas the 'super-permissive' cells had a reduced ratio of sgRNA/gRNA.
source: We estimated the sgRNA/gRNA ratio for individual cells and found that sgRNA synthesis is favoured in the 'partially resistant' and 'permissive' cells, whereas the 'super-permissive' cells had a reduced ratio of sgRNA/gRNA (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of sgRNA/gRNA ratio by cell type shown in Figure 3H.

claim: gRNA synthesis is favoured in the late phase of infection, which may reflect the requirement of gRNA to assemble new viral particles.
source: In summary, these results indicate that gRNA synthesis is favoured in the late phase of infection, which may reflect the requirement of gRNA to assemble new viral particles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed shift in sgRNA/gRNA ratio over time.

claim: 1–2 factories per cell were observed at 2 hpi, which increased to ~30 factories/cell by 10 hpi.
source: We observed 1–2 factories per cell at 2 hpi, which increased to ~30 factories/cell by 10 hpi (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of viral factories shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The average number of gRNA molecules within viral factories increased over time.
source: In addition, the average number of gRNA molecules within these factories, although variable, increased over time (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: RDV treatment reduced both the number of viral factories per cell and their RNA content.
source: RDV treatment reduced both the number of viral factories per cell and their RNA content.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of viral factory metrics in untreated and RDV-treated cells.

claim: 3–5% of A549-ACE2 and Calu-3 cells showed a 'super-permissive' phenotype.
source: In agreement with our earlier observations with Vero E6, 3–5% of A549-ACE2 and Calu-3 cells showed a 'super-permissive' phenotype (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The 'super-permissive' infected Vero E6, A549-ACE2, and Calu-3 cells were randomly distributed.
source: In summary, our results show conclusively that the 'super-permissive' infected Vero E6, A549-ACE2, and Calu-3 cells were randomly distributed (Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 4E, F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The random distribution of super-permissive cells is consistent with an intrinsic property of the cell that defines susceptibility to virus infection.
source: We interpret these data as being consistent with an intrinsic property of the cell that defines susceptibility to virus infection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the random distribution pattern of super-permissive cells.

claim: The random distribution argues against cell-to-cell signalling mechanisms that would either lead to clustering (if increasing susceptibility) or to an even distribution (if inhibiting) of infected cells.
source: The data also argue against cell-to-cell signalling mechanisms that would either lead to clustering (if increasing susceptibility) or to an even distribution (if inhibiting) of infected cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed random distribution pattern.

claim: The number of gRNA molecules at 2 hpi was similar for both B.1.1.7 and VIC viruses, reflecting similar cell uptake of viral particles.
source: We discovered that the number of gRNA molecules at 2 hpi was similar for both viruses, reflecting similar cell uptake of viral particles (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 5B–E.

claim: The quantities of intracellular gRNA and sgRNA were lower in B.1.1.7-infected cells compared to VIC at 6 and 8 hpi.
source: However, the quantities of intracellular gRNA and sgRNA were lower in B.1.1.7-infected cells compared to VIC at 6 and 8 hpi (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 5E.

claim: While the amount of gRNA per cell was reduced in the B.1.1.7 variant, there were an equal number of +ORF1a and +ORFN-positive cells.
source: We also found that while the amount of gRNA per cell was reduced in the B.1.1.7 variant, there were an equal number of +ORF1a and +ORFN-positive cells (Figure 5D), suggesting that the reduced B.1.1.7 RNA burden is due to a differential replication efficiency rather than infection rate.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The B.1.1.7 variant showed a reduced number of replication factories per cell compared to the VIC strain.
source: The B.1.1.7 variant also showed a reduced number of replication factories per cell (Figure 5F), with each focus containing on average a lower number of gRNA molecules compared to the VIC strain (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Each B.1.1.7 replication factory contained on average a lower number of gRNA molecules compared to the VIC strain.
source: The B.1.1.7 variant also showed a reduced number of replication factories per cell (Figure 5F), with each focus containing on average a lower number of gRNA molecules compared to the VIC strain (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: RDV treatment ablated the differences between the viral strains, demonstrating that the observed phenotype is replication-dependent.
source: RDV treatment ablated the differences between the viral strains, demonstrating that the observed phenotype is replication-dependent (Figure 5B,E-I).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of untreated and RDV-treated conditions shown in Figure 5B, E-I.

claim: The lower level of individual gRNA detected in RDV-treated cells persisted for at least 8 hpi in both the VIC and B.1.1.7 strains.
source: Nevertheless, the lower level of individual gRNA that we detected in RDV-treated cells persisted for at least 8 hpi in both the VIC and B.1.1.7 strains.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course analysis of gRNA in RDV-treated cells.

claim: Individual gRNA molecules of both the VIC and B.1.1.7 strains are highly stable in the cytoplasm of infected cells.
source: We conclude that individual gRNA molecules of both the strains are highly stable in the cytoplasm of infected cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the persistence of gRNA in RDV-treated cells.

claim: B.1.1.7-infected cells show lower sgRNA/gRNA ratio between 2 and 8 hpi compared to VIC.
source: Consistent with the delay in replication, we observed a shallower growth of the sgRNA/gRNA ratio in B.1.1.7-infected cells between 2 and 8 hpi compared to the VIC strain (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: B.1.1.7-infected 'partially resistant' and 'permissive' cells show lower sgRNA/gRNA ratio while 'super-permissive' cells displayed 1.5-fold higher ratio compared to VIC.
source: We noted that B.1.1.7-infected 'partially resistant' and 'permissive' cells show lower sgRNA/gRNA ratio while 'super-permissive' cells displayed 1.5-fold higher ratio compared to VIC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of sgRNA/gRNA ratio by cell type shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The frequency of super-permissive cells was lower for B.1.1.7 at 6 and 8 hpi.
source: The frequency of super-permissive cells was lower for B.1.1.7 at 6 and 8 hpi (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The distribution of super-permissive cells with B.1.1.7 was random at 8 hpi but changed to a non-random pattern at 24 hpi.
source: In agreement with our results with VIC (Figure 4E and F), the distribution of super-permissive cells with B.1.1.7 was random at 8 hpi; however, this changed to a non-random pattern at 24 hpi.
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The distribution of VIC super-permissive cells remained random at all timepoints.
source: In contrast, the distribution of VIC super-permissive cells remained random at all timepoints (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: B.1.1.7 displays a potentially higher capacity to spread locally between adjacent cells than VIC.
source: We interpret these results as demonstrating differences in the infection kinetics of the variants, with B.1.1.7 displaying a potentially higher capacity to spread locally between adjacent cells than VIC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the non-random distribution of B.1.1.7 super-permissive cells at 24 hpi.

claim: Both VIC and B.1.1.7 infections resulted in comparable numbers of infected cells and similar numbers of gRNA molecules per cell at 2 hpi in A549-ACE2 cells.
source: Both VIC and B.1.1.7 infections resulted in comparable numbers of infected cells and similar numbers of gRNA molecules per cell at 2 hpi, demonstrating a similar degree of viral particle entry into cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Infection with the B.1.1.7 variant led to a reduced gRNA and sgRNA burden at 8 and 24 hpi in A549-ACE2 cells.
source: However, infection with the B.1.1.7 variant led to a reduced gRNA and sgRNA burden at 8 and 24 hpi (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6A, B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Fewer 'super-permissive' cells were detected with B.1.1.7 at 8 and 24 hpi in A549-ACE2 cells.
source: Moreover, fewer 'super-permissive' cells were detected at these timepoints (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A modest but significant reduction in the infectious titre of B.1.1.7 compared to VIC was found at 8 and 24 hpi.
source: We found a modest but significant reduction in the infectious titre of B.1.1.7 compared to VIC at 8 and 24 hpi, consistent with the reduced cellular RNA burden of B.1.1.7.
evidence: The claim is supported by plaque forming assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The replication and secretion rates of B.1.1.7 are slower than VIC in contrast to its more rapid spread in the human population.
source: Considering these results together, we conclude that the replication and secretion rates of B.1.1.7 are slower than VIC in contrast to its more rapid spread in the human population.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined smFISH and infectious virus release data.

claim: Similar levels of vRNA were detected at 2 hpi within B.1.1.7 or VIC-infected A549-ACE2 cells, consistent with similar internalisation rates.
source: In agreement with our smFISH analysis, we detected similar levels of vRNA at 2 hpi within B.1.1.7 or VIC-infected cells, consistent with similar internalisation rates in A549-ACE2 cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The abundance of vRNAs in B.1.1.7-infected cells at 8 and 24 hpi was notably lower than with VIC-infected cells.
source: However, the abundance of vRNAs in B.1.1.7-infected cells at 8 and 24 hpi was notably lower than with VIC-infected cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The level of B.1.1.7 RNA was almost unaltered between 2 and 8 hpi, and then increased dramatically at 24 hpi.
source: Furthermore, the level of B.1.1.7 RNA was almost unaltered between 2 and 8 hpi, and then increased dramatically at 24 hpi (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), contrasting with VIC-infected cells, which showed a continuous increase in vRNA over time.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: VIC-infected cells showed a continuous increase in vRNA over time.
source: Furthermore, the level of B.1.1.7 RNA was almost unaltered between 2 and 8 hpi, and then increased dramatically at 24 hpi (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), contrasting with VIC-infected cells, which showed a continuous increase in vRNA over time.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Negative sense viral RNAs represent a small fraction of the vRNA present in the cell.
source: Negative sense viral RNAs represent a small fraction of the vRNA present in the cell, as assayed by smFISH (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Negative sense transcripts are detectable as early as 2 hpi.
source: These negative sense transcripts are detectable as early as 2 hpi, adding further support to our earlier conclusion that primary viral replication events can occur rapidly post-infection, particularly in 'super-permissive' cells (Figures 3C and 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The ratio between negative and positive sense vRNAs increased throughout the infection for the VIC strain.
source: The ratio between negative and positive sense vRNAs increased throughout the infection for the VIC strain, but for B.1.1.7 we observed a modest reduction in the ratio at 24 hpi (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: For B.1.1.7, a modest reduction in the negative to positive sense vRNA ratio was observed at 24 hpi.
source: The ratio between negative and positive sense vRNAs increased throughout the infection for the VIC strain, but for B.1.1.7 we observed a modest reduction in the ratio at 24 hpi (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: sgRNAs were detected in low quantities at 2 hpi.
source: In agreement with smFISH data, sgRNAs were detected in low quantities at 2 hpi (Figure 6D and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6D and G.

claim: For VIC, the sgRNA/gRNA ratio peaks at 8 hpi, followed by a significant drop at 24 hpi.
source: For VIC, the sgRNA/gRNA ratio peaks at 8 hpi, followed by a significant drop at 24 hpi (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: For B.1.1.7, a significantly lower sgRNA/gRNA ratio was observed at 8 hpi when compared to VIC.
source: For B.1.1.7, we observed a significantly lower sgRNA/gRNA ratio at 8 hpi when compared to VIC (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The sgRNA/gRNA ratio of B.1.1.7 remained stable between 8 and 24 hpi, surpassing VIC.
source: However, the sgRNA/gRNA ratio of B.1.1.7 remained stable between 8 and 24 hpi, surpassing VIC (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Both VIC and B.1.1.7 have different kinetics of gRNA and sgRNA expression.
source: These results suggest that both VIC and B.1.1.7 have a different kinetics of gRNA and sgRNA expression, complementing our earlier observations with smFISH (Figure 3C and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and is consistent with smFISH observations.

claim: S-sgRNA was the dominant species at 2 hpi, while the sgRNA encoding N (N-sgRNA) become prevalent at 8–24 hpi.
source: We found that S-sgRNA was the dominant species at 2 hpi, while the sgRNA encoding N (N-sgRNA) become prevalent at 8–24 hpi (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis of individual sgRNA species shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The early S-to-N sgRNA switch upon infection indicates a transition to the assembly of viral particles requiring large numbers of N molecules.
source: We interpret this early S-to-N sgRNA switch upon infection as indicating a transition to the assembly of viral particles requiring large numbers of N molecules.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed shift in sgRNA expression and knowledge of viral assembly requirements.

claim: At 2 hpi, B.1.1.7 produced more S-sgRNA but less N-sgRNA than VIC.
source: At 2 hpi, B.1.1.7 produced more S-sgRNA but less N-sgRNA than VIC, which is consistent with a delayed B.1.1.7 replication kinetic and S-to-N transition.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis of individual sgRNA species.

claim: Upregulation of sgRNAs encoding ORF9b (~0.13%) and N* (~1%) was found in B.1.1.7-infected cells.
source: Furthermore, we found upregulation of sgRNAs encoding ORF9b (~0.13%) and N* (~1%) in B.1.1.7-infected cells (Figure 6I), in agreement with recent studies reporting altered sgRNA landscapes for B.1.1.7 (Parker et al., 2021; Thorne et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6I and is consistent with recent studies (Parker et al., 2021; Thorne et al., 2021).

claim: Upregulation of ORF9b and N* transcripts is likely to result from advantageous mutations that create novel transcriptional regulatory sequences (TRS-B) in B.1.1.7.
source: Upregulation of these transcripts is likely to result from advantageous mutations that create novel transcriptional regulatory sequences (TRS-B) in B.1.1.7 (Parker et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed upregulation and is supported by cited studies (Parker et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).

claim: Mutations in TRS-B near N* were also found in P.1 (Gamma) and P.2 (Zeta) variants while mutations in TRS-B near ORF9b were unique to B.1.1.7.
source: When we scanned for the TRS motifs in other VOCs and variants of interests (VOIs), we found mutations in TRS-B near N* were also found in P.1 (Gamma) and P.2 (Zeta) variants while mutations in TRS-B near ORF9b were unique to B.1.1.7 (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis of TRS motifs across variants.

claim: Multiple sequence alignment of VOCs and VOIs revealed that mutations accumulate frequently at or near the TRS motif sequences.
source: However, multiple sequence alignment of VOCs and VOIs revealed that mutations accumulate frequently at or near the TRS motif sequences, suggesting that SARS-CoV-2 utilises these regulatory motif and surrounding sequences as evolutionary hotspots to modulate sgRNA expression and viral fitness.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and is inferred to have functional significance.

claim: B.1.1.7 does not only exhibit delayed replication kinetics, but also produces a differential pool of sgRNAs likely due to mutations within the TRS.
source: These transcriptomic results reveal that B.1.1.7 does not only exhibit delayed replication kinetics, but also produces a differential pool of sgRNAs likely due to mutations within the TRS.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of delayed replication and altered sgRNA expression.

claim: smFISH is a sensitive approach that allows the absolute quantification of SARS-CoV-2 RNAs at single-molecule resolution.
source: In this study, we show that smFISH is a sensitive approach that allows the absolute quantification of SARS-CoV-2 RNAs at single-molecule resolution.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results demonstrating single-molecule detection.

claim: smFISH experiments show the detection of individual gRNA molecules within the first 2 hr of infection, which most likely reflect incoming viral particles.
source: Our experiments show the detection of individual gRNA molecules within the first 2 hr of infection, which most likely reflect incoming viral particles.
evidence: The claim is supported by smFISH data at 2 hpi and is inferred from the timing and RDV insensitivity.

claim: Small numbers of foci comprising several gRNAs sensitive to RDV treatment were observed at 2 hpi, demonstrating early replication events.
source: However, we also observed small numbers of foci comprising several gRNAs sensitive to RDV treatment, demonstrating early replication events.
evidence: The claim is supported by smFISH observations at 2 hpi and RDV sensitivity.

claim: The multi-gRNA foci represent 'replication factories' as they co-stain with FISH probes specific for negative sense viral RNA and sgRNA.
source: We believe that these foci represent 'replication factories' as they co-stain with FISH probes specific for negative sense viral RNA and sgRNA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-localization of positive and negative strand RNA and sgRNA.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 replication occurs within the first 2 hr of infection and increases over time.
source: These data provide the first evidence that SARS-CoV-2 replication occurs within the first 2 hr of infection and increases over time.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course smFISH data showing increasing gRNA and replication factories.

claim: Viral-dependent J2 signals were apparent at 6 hpi.
source: This contrasts to our observations with the J2 anti-dsRNA antibody where viral-dependent signals were apparent at 6 hpi (Cortese et al., 2020; Eymieux et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by J2 antibody staining data and is consistent with cited studies (Cortese et al., 2020; Eymieux et al., 2021).

claim: Co-staining SARS-CoV-2-infected cells with J2 antibody and +ORF1a smFISH probe showed a partial overlap, suggesting that infection may induce changes in cellular dsRNA.
source: We noted that co-staining SARS-CoV-2-infected cells with J2 antibody and +ORF1a with an smFISH probe set showed a partial overlap, suggesting that infection may induce changes in cellular dsRNA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the partial overlap between J2 and smFISH signals.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 gRNA persisted in the presence of RDV, suggesting a long half-life that may reflect the high secondary structure of the RNA genome that could render it refractory to the action of nucleases.
source: We found that SARS-CoV-2 gRNA persisted in the presence of RDV, suggesting a long half-life that may reflect the high secondary structure of the RNA genome that could render it refractory to the action of nucleases (Huston et al., 2021; Simmonds et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the persistence of gRNA in RDV-treated cells and is supported by cited studies on RNA structure (Huston et al., 2021; Simmonds et al., 2021).

claim: The high synthesis of sgRNAs aims to fulfil the high demand for structural proteins in the viral particles.
source: Since a viral particle is composed of thousands of proteins and a single RNA molecule, we interpret the high synthesis of sgRNAs as aiming to fulfil the high demand for structural proteins in the viral particles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed high sgRNA levels and knowledge of viral particle composition.

claim: The late shift towards gRNA synthesis may ensure the presence of sufficient gRNA to generate the viral progeny.
source: Once the structural proteins are available in sufficient quantities, the late shift towards gRNA synthesis may ensure the presence of sufficient gRNA to generate the viral progeny.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed shift in sgRNA/gRNA ratio over time.

claim: Cells vary in their susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection, where most cells had low vRNA levels (<102 copies/cell), but a minor population (4–10% depending on the cell line) had much higher vRNA burden (>105 copies/cell) at 10 hpi.
source: Our study shows that cells vary in their susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 infection, where most cells had low vRNA levels (<102 copies/cell), but a minor population (4–10% depending on the cell line) had much higher vRNA burden (>105 copies/cell) at 10 hpi.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of vRNA distribution across cell populations.

claim: The number of intracellular vRNA copies at 2 hpi was similar across the culture, suggesting that the super-permissive phenotype is not explained by differences in virus entry.
source: In contrast, the number of intracellular vRNA copies at 2 hpi was similar across the culture, suggesting that this phenotype is not explained by differences in virus entry.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similar vRNA levels at 2 hpi across all cells.

claim: 'Super-permissive' cells account for the majority of vRNA within the culture and mask the dominant cell population.
source: These 'super-permissive' cells account for the majority of vRNA within the culture and mask the dominant cell population.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of total vRNA contribution by cell type.

claim: The variable susceptibility is unlikely to reflect differential immune cell signalling as both Calu-3 and A549-ACE2 have intact innate sensing pathways unlike Vero cells.
source: As both Calu-3 and A549-ACE2 have intact innate sensing pathways (Cao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021) unlike Vero cells (Desmyter et al., 1968), this variable susceptibility is unlikely to reflect differential immune cell signalling and is consistent with their random distribution within the culture.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of similar heterogeneity in cells with different immune capabilities and is supported by cited studies (Cao et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Desmyter et al., 1968).

claim: The reason for the differential infection fitness may rely on the intrinsic properties of each cell, including the stage of the cell cycle, the expression of individual antiviral sensors or the metabolic state.
source: The reason for the differential infection fitness may rely on the intrinsic properties of each cell, including the stage of the cell cycle, the expression of individual antiviral sensors or the metabolic state.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential mechanisms for the observed heterogeneity.

claim: Recent single-cell RNA sequencing studies of SARS-CoV-2-infected bronchial cultures identified ciliated cells as the primary target.
source: Recent single-cell RNA sequencing studies of SARS-CoV-2-infected bronchial cultures identified ciliated cells as the primary target.
evidence: The claim is based on cited single-cell RNA sequencing studies.

claim: Only a minority of ciliated cells contained vRNA that may either reflect low sequencing depth or cell-to-cell variation in susceptibility.
source: However, only a minority of these cells contained vRNA that may either reflect low sequencing depth or cell-to-cell variation in susceptibility (Fiege et al., 2021; Ravindra et al., 2021), and indeed, our smFISH results on experimentally infected hamster lungs showed variable RNA levels across the tissue (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from cited studies (Fiege et al., 2021; Ravindra et al., 2021) and is consistent with smFISH observations in hamster lungs.

claim: Most studies on emergent VOC have focused on mutations mapping to the Spike glycoprotein as they can alter virus attachment, entry, and sensitivity to vaccine-induced or naturally acquired neutralising antibodies.
source: Most studies have focused on mutations mapping to the Spike glycoprotein as they can alter virus attachment, entry, and sensitivity to vaccine-induced or naturally acquired neutralising antibodies.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge of the field and cited studies.

claim: Many of the mutations in VOC map to other viral proteins, including components of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase complex that could impact RNA replication, and non-coding regulatory regions as the TRSs, which can affect sgRNA expression.
source: However, many of the mutations map to other viral proteins, including components of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase complex that could impact RNA replication, and non-coding regulatory regions as the TRSs, which can affect sgRNA expression.
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis of VOC mutations.

claim: The B.1.1.7 variant shows slower replication kinetics compared to the VIC strain, resulting in lower gRNA and sgRNA copies per cell, fewer viral replication factories and a reduced frequency of 'super-permissive' cells.
source: Our smFISH analysis revealed that the B.1.1.7 variant shows slower replication kinetics compared to the VIC strain, resulting in lower gRNA and sgRNA copies per cell, fewer viral replication factories and a reduced frequency of 'super-permissive' cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive smFISH analysis comparing B.1.1.7 and VIC.

claim: The delay in B.1.1.7 replication was observed in Vero and A549-ACE2 cells and was confirmed by RNA-seq as an orthogonal method.
source: This delay in B.1.1.7 replication was observed in Vero and A549-ACE2 cells and was confirmed by RNA-seq as an orthogonal method.
evidence: The claim is supported by both smFISH and RNA-seq data in multiple cell types.

claim: Emerging VOCs, such as B.1.1.7, have been reported to have a fitness advantage in terms of their ability to transmit compared to the VIC isolate.
source: Emerging VOCs, such as B.1.1.7, have been reported to have a fitness advantage in terms of their ability to transmit compared to the VIC isolate (Caly et al., 2020; Davies et al., 2021; Kidd et al., 2021; Volz et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on cited epidemiological studies (Caly et al., 2020; Davies et al., 2021; Kidd et al., 2021; Volz et al., 2021).

claim: A recent study reported that B.1.1.7 leads to higher levels of intracellular vRNA and N protein than VIC at 24 and 48 hpi using 'in-bulk' RT-qPCR and immunofluorescence.
source: Interestingly, a recent study reported that B.1.1.7 leads to higher levels of intracellular vRNA and N protein than VIC at 24 and 48 hpi using 'in-bulk' RT-qPCR and immunofluorescence, respectively (Thorne et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on a cited study (Thorne et al., 2021).

claim: While B.1.1.7 still produces lower level of vRNA than VIC at 24 hpi, it exhibits a clear recovery compared to 8 hpi.
source: We observed that while B.1.1.7 still produces lower level of vRNA than VIC at 24 hpi (Figure 6E), it exhibits a clear recovery compared to 8 hpi.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: It is plausible that both variants yield similar total amounts of viral RNA and proteins but within a different time frame.
source: It is thus plausible that both variants yield similar total amounts of viral RNA and proteins but within a different time frame.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential explanation for the observed differences.

claim: 'In-bulk' RT-qPCR analysis does not provide absolute quantification and individual cell assessment and, therefore, should likely be biased towards the super-susceptible cells that account for most of the RNA burden.
source: That said, 'in-bulk' RT-qPCR analysis does not provide absolute quantification and individual cell assessment and, therefore, should likely be biased towards the super-susceptible cells that account for most of the RNA burden.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the understanding of bulk vs. single-cell methods and the observed heterogeneity.

claim: Thorne and colleagues reported an elevated expression of the sgRNA encoding the innate agonist ORF9b.
source: Thorne and colleagues also reported an elevated expression of the sgRNA encoding the innate agonist ORF9b (Thorne et al., 2021), which is also supported by our results.
evidence: The claim is based on a cited study (Thorne et al., 2021) and is supported by the authors' own data.

claim: Enhanced ORF9b expression, together with the lower intracellular vRNA levels present in B.1.1.7-infected cells, may grant this variant with an advantage to evade the antiviral response.
source: Enhanced ORF9b expression, together with the lower intracellular vRNA levels present in B.1.1.7-infected cells, may grant this variant with an advantage to evade the antiviral response.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential mechanism for B.1.1.7's fitness advantage.

claim: This advantage, combined with mutations in the Spike that are proposed to improve cell entry, could provide the B.1.1.7 with a replicative advantage over the early lineage VIC strain enabling its rapid dissemination across the human population.
source: This advantage, combined with mutations in the Spike that are proposed to improve cell entry, could provide the B.1.1.7 with a replicative advantage over the early lineage VIC strain enabling its rapid dissemination across the human population (Caly et al., 2020; Davies et al., 2021; Kidd et al., 2021; Volz et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a combined mechanism for B.1.1.7's increased transmission, and is supported by cited studies (Caly et al., 2020; Davies et al., 2021; Kidd et al., 2021; Volz et al., 2021).

claim: A recent longitudinal study of nasopharyngeal swabs showed that the B.1.1.7 variant was associated with longer infection times and yet showed similar peak viral loads to non-B.1.1.7 variants.
source: A recent longitudinal study of nasopharyngeal swabs showed that the B.1.1.7 variant was associated with longer infection times and yet showed similar peak viral loads to non-B.1.1.7 variants (Kissler et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on a cited study (Kissler et al., 2021).

claim: The extended duration of virus shedding may contribute to increased transmissibility and is consistent with data showing reduced replication of B.1.1.7 at the single-cell level.
source: The authors conclude that this extended duration of virus shedding may contribute to increased transmissibility and is consistent with our data showing reduced replication of B.1.1.7 at the single-cell level.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cited study's conclusions and the authors' own data.

claim: An independent study reported a significantly longer duration of SARS-CoV-2 RNA in nasopharyngeal swabs from persons infected with B.1.1.7 (16 days) compared to those infected with other lineages (14 days).
source: An independent study reported a significantly longer duration of SARS-CoV-2 RNA in nasopharyngeal swabs from persons infected with B.1.1.7 (16 days) compared to those infected with other lineages (14 days) (Calistri et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on a cited study (Calistri et al., 2021).

claim: Lower replication may allow the virus to replicate and persist for longer periods before host antiviral sensors are triggered.
source: In contrast, lower replication may allow the virus to replicate and persist for longer periods before host antiviral sensors are triggered.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential mechanism for the observed longer infection duration.

claim: Differences in replication fitness and their impact on host antiviral responses are likely to be of key importance for understanding the success of viral variants to spread through the population.
source: Such differences, and their impact on host antiviral responses, are likely to be of key importance for our understanding of the success of viral variants to spread through the population.
evidence: The claim is a general statement about the importance of the findings.
